baseline: Host Linux: open04 passes with 1 TPASS. The test sets RLIMIT_NOFILE, opens files until the limit is reached, then verifies the next open(2) returns EMFILE (errno 24). Test output: 'open04.c:52: TPASS: open(fname, O_RDWR | O_CREAT, 0777) : EMFILE (24)'
failing_assertion: The test fails on Asterinas (0 passed / 1 failed per kirk summary). The open(2) call that should return EMFILE succeeds instead, allocating a file descriptor beyond RLIMIT_NOFILE
root_cause: FileTable::insert (line 190) unconditionally calls self.table.put(entry) without consulting RLIMIT_NOFILE. The comment at line 192 states 'Resource limits guarantee the table never exceeds i32::MAX entries' but this guarantee is not enforced—the check is entirely absent. When open.rs:63 calls file_table_locked.insert(...), the fd is allocated regardless of whether the process has reached its RLIMIT_NOFILE soft limit.
invariant: A process must not be able to allocate a file descriptor with value >= RLIMIT_NOFILE (soft limit). Any syscall that allocates a new fd—open, openat, creat, dup, fcntl(F_DUPFD), pipe, socket, accept, etc.—must return EMFILE when the next available fd number would equal or exceed the limit.
owning_layer: File descriptor allocator: FileTable::insert and FileTable::dup_ceil in kernel/src/fs/file/file_table.rs. This is the VFS-equivalent layer above individual file types, analogous to Linux's __alloc_fd in fs/file.c.
linux_reference: Linux enforces RLIMIT_NOFILE in __alloc_fd (fs/file.c, around line 480-510 in recent kernels). When expanding the fd table or finding the next free fd, it checks 'if (fd >= rlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE)) return -EMFILE;' before the actual allocation. This happens in the generic fd allocator, so every syscall that allocates an fd inherits the check. See also alloc_fd which wraps __alloc_fd with start=0.
other_callers: Every syscall that allocates a new fd is affected. In Asterinas: (1) open.rs:63 / sys_openat calls insert—the path tested by open04. (2) dup.rs:16 / sys_dup calls dup_ceil with no prior check—dup(2) can also bypass the limit. (3) fcntl.rs likely uses dup_ceil for F_DUPFD / F_DUPFD_CLOEXEC. (4) pipe.rs, socket.rs, accept.rs, eventfd.rs, timerfd.rs, signalfd.rs, and any other syscall that calls FileTable::insert. The defect is in the allocator itself, so it affects the entire fd allocation surface.
suggested_direction: Add RLIMIT_NOFILE enforcement to FileTable::insert and FileTable::dup_ceil. For insert: before calling self.table.put, compute the next fd that would be allocated (self.table.slots_len() if the last slot is occupied, else the first free slot's index), check if that value >= rlimit(RLIMIT_NOFILE).get_cur(), and return Errno::EMFILE if so. For dup_ceil: after computing min_free_fd at line 162, check if min_free_fd >= rlimit before calling put_at. Both methods need access to the process's resource limits, which currently they do not have—FileTable has no reference to the process. Options: (A) Pass the Context down through all file_table call sites and add a ctx parameter to insert/dup_ceil. (B) Store a weak reference to the process or resource limits in FileTable (set at construction). (C) Move the check to the syscall layer—before every insert/dup_ceil call, verify the anticipated fd < rlimit. Option C is simpler but duplicates the check across many syscalls; option A is architecturally cleaner and matches Linux's design (single enforcement point in the allocator). Whichever path is chosen, ensure the check uses get_cur() (soft limit) not get_max() (hard limit), and that the errno is EMFILE for all affected syscalls (dup/fcntl return EMFILE per POSIX, not EBADF).
